title: Emergency drugs, oxygen & equipment checks
blurb: What's in the practice emergency kit, what each drug is for, and how the team checks, logs and replaces it.
question: It's your turn to do the weekly emergency kit check. You find the oxygen cylinder gauge reading low, the glucagon expires next week, and the check log hasn't been signed for three weeks. What do you do about each problem?

teach.h: A kit that is complete, in date and known to all
teach.body: Every dental practice keeps a set of emergency drugs and equipment so the team can treat the common emergencies until the ambulance arrives. It only works if three things are true: everything is there, everything is in date and working, and every member of staff knows where it is from their first day. When a patient collapses anywhere in the building, the runner brings the emergency drugs kit, the oxygen and the AED together.

teach.caption: Based on SDCEP's list, which also includes an oral antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine, chlorphenamine or loratadine) for mild allergic reactions.

teach.caption: Injected into the outer middle third of the thigh. Repeat after 5 minutes if there's no improvement (RCUK 2021).

teach.body: Adult doses you should recognise: GTN 2 puffs under the tongue, repeated after 5 minutes if pain continues. Aspirin 300 mg chewed for a suspected heart attack (not for under-16s). Salbutamol 1 puff every 30–60 seconds through a spacer, up to 10 puffs. Oral glucose 15–20 g for a conscious hypo patient, or glucagon 1 mg IM if they can't swallow safely. Buccal midazolam 10 mg (2 mL) for a convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more. Who gives each drug follows the practice protocol and each person's training; usually the dentist leads while you prepare and hand over.

teach.caption: The cylinder must hold enough to keep giving 15 L/min until the ambulance arrives. A low reading is reported and the cylinder replaced.

teach.h: Equipment that must be available immediately (RCUK)

rows.label: Self-inflating bag with reservoir (adult and child) + clear masks 0–4

teach.note: RCUK asks for single-patient-use, latex-free items where feasible, and a standard AED sign so the defibrillator is found quickly.

items: Check every drug is present, sealed and in date. Note anything expiring soon.
Check the oxygen: cylinder content gauge, tubing and masks present.
Check the AED: status indicator OK, pads present and in date, spare set there.
Check suction works and airways, bag-valve-mask and pocket mask are all present.
Record the check on the log: date, findings, your signature.
Report and replace anything used, low, missing or near expiry, and record that too.

items.label: Know where the kit is
items.sub: Every new starter, before seeing patients

items.label: Kit check by named people
items.sub: With cover for absence; logged and audited

items.label: Restock and record
items.sub: Kit must be complete for the next emergency

items.label: Planned replacement
items.sub: Order replacements early using the log

items.label: Team training
items.sub: GDC recommends at least 2 h of medical emergencies CPD a year

teach.text: "1:1000" means 1 mg in 1 mL, so 0.5 mL contains 500 micrograms. Don't confuse micrograms (µg) with milligrams (mg): 500 µg is 0.5 mg. And a kit that is complete but locked away, or whose location nobody knows, fails in an emergency just as badly as an empty one.

items: Drugs: adrenaline 1:1000, aspirin 300 mg, GTN 400 µg/dose, salbutamol 100 µg, glucagon 1 mg, oral glucose, buccal midazolam, oxygen.
Adult adrenaline IM 500 µg (0.5 mL); child 6–12 years 300 µg; repeat after 5 minutes if needed.
Oxygen 15 L/min; a full CD cylinder (460 L) lasts about 30 minutes.
Checks at least weekly by named people, logged, with planned replacement before expiry.
Everyone knows where the kit is from day one; restock immediately after use.

summary: You can now list the emergency drugs in a dental practice with their forms, routes and uses, recall the adrenaline doses by age and key adult doses, explain oxygen requirements, name the RCUK immediate equipment, and carry out and record a weekly kit check, including what to do about low oxygen or drugs near expiry.

A.q: A colleague calls for help because a patient has collapsed in the waiting room. What is most important to bring with you?
options: A blood pressure monitor and cuff
The emergency drugs kit and the AED
A clinical waste bag and gloves
A.why: For any collapse, the emergency drugs kit, oxygen and AED should be brought straight away so the team can treat whatever they find.

whyNot.0: The history is useful later, but it can't treat the patient.
whyNot.1: A blood pressure reading won't help a patient in cardiac arrest.
whyNot.3: Waste disposal isn't a priority in the first minutes of an emergency.

A.q: Which form of adrenaline is kept in the dental emergency kit for intramuscular use in anaphylaxis?
A.why: The dental kit holds adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000), as ampoules or prefilled syringes, for IM injection.

whyNot.1: 1:10,000 is a weaker strength and is not the IM form in the dental kit.
whyNot.2: 1:100 is ten times too strong and is not used.
whyNot.3: This is far too weak; strengths like this are found in some local anaesthetic cartridges, not the emergency kit.

A.q: During the weekly check, you notice the oxygen cylinder gauge is reading low. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Leave it, as it still has some oxygen
Record it and report it for replacement
Mention it at next month's team meeting
Move it to the back of the cupboard
A.why: A low cylinder may not last until an ambulance arrives, so record it on the log and report it so it is replaced promptly.

whyNot.0: A part-empty cylinder may run out during an emergency.
whyNot.2: Waiting a month leaves the practice without enough oxygen.
whyNot.3: Hiding the problem doesn't solve it and could delay an emergency response.

B.q: According to RCUK, how often should a dental practice's resuscitation equipment be checked as a minimum?
B.why: RCUK says checks should be at least weekly, carried out by named individuals with cover for absence.

whyNot.0: Daily checks are fine if local policy wants them, but the RCUK minimum is weekly.
whyNot.2: Monthly is less often than the RCUK minimum.
whyNot.3: Six-monthly checks would leave expired or used items unnoticed for far too long.

B.q: The dentist asks for the drug used for an angina attack. What should you hand them?
B.why: Angina is treated with GTN spray (400 micrograms per dose) under the tongue.

whyNot.0: Aspirin is given for a suspected heart attack, not routine angina.
whyNot.2: Glucagon treats hypoglycaemia in a patient who can't take sugar by mouth.

B.q: A patient with diabetes is shaky and sweaty but conscious and able to swallow. Which item from the kit is used first?
B.why: A conscious hypoglycaemic patient who can swallow is given oral glucose (15–20 g for an adult).

whyNot.0: Glucagon is for a patient who is unconscious or can't swallow safely.

C.q: A practice reviews its emergency preparedness after a near miss. Which shortcoming is most serious?
options: The check log uses an old template
The kit bag is a different colour
Drugs are stored in alphabetical order
Some staff don't know where the kit is
C.why: If staff can't find the kit, nothing in it can be used in time. RCUK requires all staff to know where the resuscitation equipment is.

whyNot.0: An old template is a minor admin issue if checks are still done and recorded.
whyNot.1: The bag's colour doesn't affect the response.
whyNot.2: Storage order is a matter of preference; it doesn't stop the kit being used.

C.q: An 8-year-old is having an anaphylactic reaction. What dose of IM adrenaline 1:1000 is given?
C.why: Children aged 6–12 years receive 300 micrograms (0.3 mL) of 1:1000 adrenaline IM.

whyNot.1: 150 micrograms is the dose for 6 months to 6 years.
whyNot.2: 500 micrograms is the dose for adults and children over 12.
whyNot.3: 1 mg is double the adult IM dose and not used.

C.q: You are updating the practice's emergency drug stock list. Which check is most important?
options: Brand names match last year's list
Drugs are kept in alphabetical order
Expiry dates are logged and tracked
Each drug is kept in a matching box
C.why: Expired drugs may not work. Logging expiry dates lets the practice replace stock before it expires (a planned replacement programme).

whyNot.0: Brands can change; what matters is the correct drug, strength and date.
whyNot.1: Order of storage doesn't affect whether drugs work.
whyNot.3: Box size is irrelevant to patient safety.

reteach.title: Like a fire extinguisher: useless if empty or hidden
reteach.question: A fire extinguisher you can't find, or one that's empty, won't put out a fire. How does that apply to the emergency kit?

blocks.body: Nobody checks a fire extinguisher during a fire. It's checked beforehand, kept in a marked place, and refilled after use. The emergency kit is the same. You check it at least weekly and sign the log, you replace drugs before they expire, you swap a low oxygen cylinder straight away, and you restock after every use. Everyone knows where it lives, so in an emergency nobody wastes a second looking.

blocks.text: "It still has some oxygen in it" is not good enough. The cylinder must last at 15 L/min until the ambulance arrives.

explain.body: Match each drug to its emergency: adrenaline for anaphylaxis, aspirin for a heart attack, GTN for angina, salbutamol for asthma, glucose or glucagon for a hypo, midazolam for a prolonged seizure, and oxygen for most emergencies.

test.q: When is buccal midazolam given to a patient having an epileptic seizure?
options: If convulsions last 5 minutes or more
As soon as any seizure starts
Only after the seizure has fully stopped
Before treatment to prevent a seizure
test.why: Buccal midazolam is given only if a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures recur in quick succession.

whyNot.1: Most seizures stop on their own; midazolam is not given straight away.
whyNot.2: Once the seizure has stopped, midazolam isn't needed.
whyNot.3: It isn't used routinely to prevent seizures in the practice.

explain.body: Adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) IM into the outer thigh: 500 µg adults and over 12s, 300 µg for 6–12 years, 150 µg for 6 months to 6 years, 100–150 µg under 6 months. Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.

test.q: What volume of adrenaline 1:1000 gives the adult IM dose of 500 micrograms?
test.why: 1:1000 is 1 mg (1,000 micrograms) per mL, so 0.5 mL contains 500 micrograms.

whyNot.2: 5 mL would be 5 mg, ten times the dose.
whyNot.3: 1 mL would be 1 mg, double the adult dose.

explain.body: Oxygen at 15 L/min; a full CD cylinder holds 460 L and lasts about 30 minutes. RCUK immediate equipment includes a pocket mask, suction, airways, bag-valve-masks, oxygen masks and tubing, an AED with spare pads, razor, scissors and PPE.

test.q: Which item is on the RCUK list of equipment to be available immediately in a dental practice?
test.why: Portable suction (such as a Yankauer) is on the RCUK primary dental care list of immediately available equipment.

whyNot.0: A pulse oximeter is useful but isn't on the RCUK immediate list for cardiorespiratory arrest.
whyNot.1: An ECG machine isn't required in primary dental care.
whyNot.2: A nebuliser isn't on the list; asthma is treated with salbutamol via a spacer.

explain.body: Named people check the kit at least weekly, with cover for absence. Every check is recorded. Anything used, low, missing or near expiry is reported and replaced, following a planned replacement programme.

test.q: You notice the emergency glucagon expires next week. What should you do?
options: Use it on the next diabetic patient
Leave it until it has actually expired
Remove it now, leaving none in the kit
Record it and arrange a replacement
test.why: Near-expiry items are logged and replaced in good time so the kit is never without an in-date drug.

whyNot.0: Drugs are given only when clinically needed, not to use up stock.
whyNot.1: Waiting risks the kit holding an expired drug when it's needed.
whyNot.2: Removing it before a replacement arrives leaves the kit incomplete.
